mechanism: The rs429358 C allele (G on the negative strand) alters the structure and function of the ApoE protein and, together with rs7412-C, defines the APOE ε4 isoform. ApoE4 is associated with altered lipoprotein metabolism and higher LDL-C and ApoB levels, promoting cholesterol accumulation in arterial walls and increasing atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk.

The rs7412 C allele (G on the negative strand) should be interpreted together with rs429358 because these two variants define the major APOE isoforms. At rs7412, the alternative T allele contributes to the APOE ε2 isoform, which is generally associated with lower LDL-C, whereas the C allele can occur in either ε3 or ε4 and therefore should not be interpreted as an independent cardiovascular risk allele.

The rs10455872 G allele (C on the negative strand) is strongly associated with higher Lp(a) levels and is often linked to LPA alleles with fewer KIV-2 repeats and smaller apo(a) isoforms. Elevated Lp(a) promotes atherosclerotic plaque development and is causally associated with increased coronary cardiovascular risk; measured Lp(a) levels should therefore be considered alongside the genotype.

The rs3798220 C allele (G on the negative strand) is associated with higher Lp(a) levels and increased coronary cardiovascular risk, particularly in populations of European ancestry. It is often linked to LPA alleles with fewer KIV-2 repeats and smaller apo(a) isoforms, although this relationship varies across populations; measured Lp(a) levels provide important additional information for individual risk assessment.

The rs505151 G allele (C on the negative strand) causes the E670G amino-acid substitution in PCSK9 and has been associated with increased PCSK9 activity and reduced hepatic clearance of LDL particles. Carriers tend to have modestly higher LDL-C levels and an increased risk of coronary artery disease, although the effect size varies between populations.

The rs693 A allele (T on the negative strand) is a synonymous APOB variant that does not alter the ApoB amino-acid sequence, and its direct functional mechanism remains uncertain. It has been associated with modestly higher ApoB, LDL-C, total cholesterol and triglyceride levels in several populations, but its association with cardiovascular disease itself is inconsistent and should be interpreted together with measured lipid levels.

The rs3135506 C allele causes the S19W amino-acid substitution in ApoA5 and is associated with impaired APOA5 function and higher circulating triglyceride levels. Reduced ApoA5-mediated regulation of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism can impair their clearance, increasing susceptibility to hypertriglyceridemia and associated cardiovascular risk.

The rs662799 G allele (C on the negative strand), commonly described as the APOA5 −1131C allele, is strongly associated with higher fasting triglyceride levels. It lies in the APOA5 promoter region, but its precise functional mechanism is not fully established and may partly reflect linkage with other functional variants in the APOA5/APOC3 locus; the triglyceride effect is particularly well established in East Asian populations.

The rs328 G allele is the protective S447X (Ser447Ter) variant, which truncates the LPL protein by two amino acids at its C-terminus. It is associated with enhanced triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism, resulting in lower triglycerides, higher HDL-C and a modest reduction in coronary heart disease risk, although the precise molecular mechanism underlying the functional gain remains incompletely defined.

The rs780094 T allele (A on the negative strand) is associated with altered regulation of hepatic glucokinase, promoting greater hepatic glucose utilization and triglyceride synthesis. Carriers typically have higher circulating triglyceride levels, despite tending to have lower fasting glucose.

The rs174547 C allele (G on the negative strand) is associated with lower FADS1-related desaturase activity and reduced conversion of dietary precursor fatty acids into longer-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). Carriers tend to have higher levels of precursors such as linoleic and α-linolenic acid and lower levels of downstream long-chain PUFAs. This is relevant to cardiovascular health because long-chain omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids influence lipid metabolism, vascular function and inflammatory processes.

The rs1535 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower FADS2-related desaturase activity and reduced endogenous conversion of dietary omega-3 and omega-6 precursor fatty acids into longer-chain PUFAs. This can influence the availability of biologically active long-chain fatty acids involved in lipid regulation and inflammatory signalling.

The rs10757278 G allele (C on the negative strand) lies within the chromosome 9p21 regulatory region and is associated with altered regulation of ANRIL and the nearby CDKN2A/CDKN2B genes. These changes can influence vascular smooth-muscle cell proliferation and other cellular processes involved in atherosclerotic plaque development, contributing to increased coronary artery disease risk.

The rs9349379 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with increased endothelin-1 signalling, a pathway involved in the regulation of vascular tone and endothelial function. Higher endothelin-1 activity can promote vasoconstriction and impaired coronary microvascular function, providing a potential mechanism linking this allele to increased coronary vascular disease risk.

The rs6025 T allele (A on the negative strand), known as Factor V Leiden, causes an Arg-to-Gln substitution that makes activated factor V resistant to normal inactivation by activated protein C. Factor V therefore remains procoagulant for longer, increasing thrombin generation and substantially increasing the risk of venous thromboembolism, particularly when combined with other acquired or genetic thrombotic risk factors.

The rs1799963 A allele (T on the negative strand), known as the prothrombin G20210A variant, increases prothrombin (factor II) production and circulating prothrombin levels. This promotes greater thrombin generation and increases blood clotting tendency, substantially increasing the risk of venous thromboembolism, particularly in combination with other genetic or acquired thrombotic risk factors.

The rs1801133 A allele (T on the negative strand), commonly known as MTHFR C677T, causes the Ala222Val substitution and reduces MTHFR enzyme activity. This can impair folate-dependent homocysteine metabolism and contribute to higher homocysteine levels, particularly when folate status is low.

The rs1801131 G allele (C on the negative strand), commonly known as MTHFR A1298C, causes the Glu429Ala substitution and is associated with moderately reduced MTHFR enzyme activity. Its effect on homocysteine is generally small when present alone but may become more relevant in combination with other MTHFR variants or suboptimal folate status.

The rs699 G allele (C on the negative strand) causes the M235T amino-acid substitution in angiotensinogen, a precursor of angiotensin II in the renin–angiotensin system that regulates vascular tone, sodium balance and blood pressure. This allele has been associated with altered angiotensinogen regulation and increased susceptibility to hypertension, although the effect is small and varies between populations.

The rs4961 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the Gly460Trp substitution in ADD1 and has been associated with increased renal sodium reabsorption and greater salt sensitivity. This may increase susceptibility to higher blood pressure, particularly in individuals with high dietary sodium intake, although the effect varies between populations.

The rs5186 C allele (G on the negative strand), commonly known as AGTR1 A1166C, is associated with altered regulation of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor and potentially greater responsiveness to angiotensin II. Enhanced angiotensin II signalling can promote vasoconstriction, sodium retention and vascular remodelling, contributing to higher blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

The rs1799983 T allele (A on the negative strand), known as the NOS3 Glu298Asp variant, changes the endothelial nitric oxide synthase protein and has been associated with reduced nitric oxide production or bioavailability. Lower nitric oxide availability can impair endothelial-dependent vasodilation, potentially increasing susceptibility to endothelial dysfunction and elevated blood pressure.

The rs4845625 T allele (A on the negative strand) in IL6R has been associated with higher circulating C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, consistent with altered IL-6 inflammatory signalling. The same allele has also been associated with higher LDL cholesterol and ApoB levels, linking this variant to a more pro-inflammatory and atherogenic metabolic profile.

The rs3918242 T allele (A on the negative strand) in the MMP9 promoter has been associated with increased promoter activity and higher MMP-9 expression. Increased MMP-9 activity can enhance extracellular matrix degradation and vascular remodeling, potentially contributing to atherosclerotic plaque instability and cardiovascular disease. Associations with coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction appear to be stronger in Asian, particularly East Asian populations.

The rs2200733 T allele (A on the negative strand) at the 4q25 locus near PITX2 is strongly associated with increased susceptibility to atrial fibrillation. This regulatory region interacts with PITX2, a transcription factor essential for atrial development and electrical function, and risk variation at this locus can alter PITX2-dependent regulation and atrial calcium homeostasis, promoting an arrhythmogenic substrate.

The rs7193343 T allele (A on the negative strand) near ZFHX3 has been associated with a modestly increased susceptibility to atrial fibrillation. ZFHX3 is a transcriptional regulator involved in cardiac gene expression and atrial electrophysiology, although the functional mechanism specifically linking rs7193343 to altered ZFHX3 activity remains incompletely defined. The association appears stronger and more consistently replicated in populations of European ancestry than in Asian populations.

The rs1800562 A allele (T on the negative strand), known as HFE C282Y (p.Cys282Tyr), disrupts normal HFE protein function and impairs regulation of the hepcidin–iron homeostasis pathway, increasing intestinal iron absorption. Homozygosity for the A allele (AA) is the major genetic cause of HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis and can lead to progressive iron accumulation, although clinical penetrance is incomplete. Heterozygous carriers (GA) generally have a substantially lower risk of clinically significant iron overload.

The rs855791 A allele (T on the negative strand), encoding the TMPRSS6 Val736 variant, is associated with lower serum iron, transferrin saturation, ferritin and hemoglobin levels. TMPRSS6 encodes matriptase-2, an important regulator of hepcidin signaling, and this variant can shift iron homeostasis toward reduced iron availability and increased susceptibility to iron deficiency.

The rs7903146 T allele (A on the negative strand) in TCF7L2 is strongly associated with increased susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. The risk allele affects regulatory activity at the TCF7L2 locus and is associated with impaired pancreatic β-cell function, reduced insulin secretion and a weaker insulinotropic response to incretin hormones, contributing to impaired glucose regulation and increased diabetes risk. Chronic dysglycaemia and type 2 diabetes are major contributors to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, linking this variant indirectly to cardiovascular risk.

The rs13266634 C allele (G on the negative strand), encoding the SLC30A8 Arg325 variant, is associated with increased susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. SLC30A8 encodes the ZnT8 zinc transporter in pancreatic β-cell insulin granules, where zinc is important for insulin storage and secretion; variation at this locus can alter β-cell function and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, contributing to impaired glucose regulation. Chronic dysglycaemia and type 2 diabetes are major contributors to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, linking this variant indirectly to cardiovascular risk.

The rs5219 T allele (A on the negative strand), encoding the KCNJ11 Lys23 variant, is associated with increased susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. The variant alters ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity in pancreatic β-cells, reducing sensitivity to ATP and increasing the threshold for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which can impair glucose regulation. Chronic dysglycaemia and type 2 diabetes are major contributors to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, linking this variant indirectly to cardiovascular risk.

The rs10830963 G allele in MTNR1B is associated with higher fasting glucose levels and increased susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. The risk allele is associated with increased MTNR1B expression in pancreatic β-cells and impaired early-phase glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, linking melatonin signaling to altered glucose regulation. Chronic dysglycaemia and type 2 diabetes contribute to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, indirectly linking this variant to cardiovascular risk.

The rs9939609 A allele in the FTO locus is strongly associated with higher BMI and increased susceptibility to obesity. This variant tags a regulatory region in which obesity-associated variation can influence pathways controlling adipocyte energy storage and thermogenesis, while the association has also been linked to differences in energy intake and appetite regulation. Increased adiposity promotes insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and other cardiometabolic abnormalities, thereby contributing indirectly to increased cardiovascular disease risk.

The rs17782313 C allele (G on the negative strand) near MC4R is strongly associated with higher BMI and increased susceptibility to obesity. MC4R is a key component of hypothalamic melanocortin signaling that regulates appetite, satiety and energy balance, although the precise functional mechanism linking rs17782313 to altered MC4R signaling remains incompletely defined. Increased adiposity can promote insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and other cardiometabolic abnormalities, thereby contributing indirectly to cardiovascular disease risk.

The rs10741657 G allele (C on the negative strand) near CYP2R1 is associated with lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and increased susceptibility to vitamin D deficiency. CYP2R1 encodes a key hepatic vitamin D 25-hydroxylase required for conversion of vitamin D to 25(OH)D, although the precise functional effect of rs10741657 on CYP2R1 activity or expression remains incompletely defined. Low vitamin D status has been associated observationally with adverse cardiometabolic outcomes, but a direct causal cardiovascular effect of this variant should not be inferred.

The rs2282679 G allele (C on the negative strand) in GC is associated with lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and increased susceptibility to vitamin D deficiency. GC encodes vitamin D-binding protein (DBP), the principal carrier of vitamin D metabolites in circulation, and genetic variation at this locus can influence circulating vitamin D concentrations. Low vitamin D status has been associated with adverse cardiometabolic outcomes, although a direct causal effect on cardiovascular disease has not been established.

The rs6025 T allele (A on the negative strand), known as Factor V Leiden, causes the Arg534Gln substitution and makes factor V resistant to normal breakdown by activated protein C. Factor V therefore remains procoagulant for longer, increasing thrombin generation and the risk of venous thrombosis. This risk can be substantially amplified by estrogen exposure, particularly with combined hormonal contraception and oral menopausal hormone therapy.

The rs1799963 A allele (T on the negative strand), known as the prothrombin G20210A variant, enhances F2 mRNA 3′-end processing, resulting in increased prothrombin production and circulating prothrombin levels. Higher prothrombin availability promotes thrombin generation and increases the risk of venous thrombosis. This risk can be further amplified by estrogen-containing contraception and oral menopausal hormone therapy.

The rs1172822 T allele (A on the negative strand), located at the BRSK1-associated 19q13.4 locus, is associated with an earlier age at natural menopause, with an effect of approximately 0.4 years per allele reported in the original European GWAS. The underlying molecular mechanism has not been fully established, but the variant marks inherited differences in the timing of ovarian ageing and reproductive lifespan.

The rs4680 A allele (T on the negative strand) causes the Val158Met substitution in COMT and reduces enzyme activity. Lower COMT activity can slow the methylation of catechol estrogens into methoxyestrogens, altering estrogen metabolite balance and potentially increasing exposure to biologically active catechol estrogen metabolites.

The rs1056836 C allele is part of the CYP1B1 Val432Leu polymorphism, which alters the activity of CYP1B1, an enzyme involved in oxidative estrogen metabolism. Differences in CYP1B1 activity can modify the pattern and rate of estrogen hydroxylation, although the metabolic effect of this variant varies between populations and its clinical consequences remain uncertain.

The rs10818854 A allele (T on the negative strand) is an intronic DENND1A variant associated with increased susceptibility to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), including evidence from women of European and Asian ancestry. The associated DENND1A locus has also been linked to hyperandrogenic and menstrual features of PCOS, although the direct molecular effect of rs10818854 has not been established.

The rs2476601 A allele (T on the negative strand) causes the R620W substitution in PTPN22, altering regulation of immune-cell signalling and reducing normal control of autoreactive lymphocytes. This increases susceptibility to autoimmune thyroid disease, including both Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and Graves’ disease, with particularly consistent associations reported in populations of European ancestry.

The rs231775 G allele (C on the negative strand) causes the Thr17Ala substitution in CTLA-4, an immune checkpoint protein that limits T-cell activation and helps maintain immune tolerance. The variant has been associated with altered CTLA-4 function and increased susceptibility to autoimmune thyroid disease, particularly Graves’ disease and, in some populations, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

The rs1801133 A allele (T on the negative strand), commonly known as MTHFR C677T, reduces the activity of the MTHFR enzyme, which is important for normal folate metabolism. Reduced enzyme activity can contribute to higher homocysteine levels, particularly when folate intake or status is low, and may affect biological processes that depend on folate and normal methylation.

The rs1801131 G allele (C on the negative strand), commonly known as MTHFR A1298C, moderately reduces MTHFR enzyme activity and can influence normal folate metabolism. Its effect is generally smaller than that of MTHFR C677T but may become more relevant when combined with other MTHFR variants or low folate status.

The rs10741657 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main marker of vitamin D status. CYP2R1 plays an important role in vitamin D metabolism, and carriers of the G allele have a modestly increased susceptibility to low vitamin D levels. Maintaining adequate vitamin D status becomes particularly important during peri- and postmenopause, when declining estrogen levels accelerate bone loss.

The rs2282679 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. The GC gene encodes vitamin D-binding protein, which transports vitamin D metabolites in the circulation, and variation at this locus can influence vitamin D status. Adequate vitamin D levels are particularly important during peri- and postmenopause, when declining estrogen levels increase susceptibility to bone loss.

The rs1800562 A allele (T on the negative strand), known as HFE C282Y, alters the HFE protein and can increase intestinal iron absorption, leading to progressive iron accumulation. The effect is strongly genotype-dependent, with the greatest risk of hereditary hemochromatosis in individuals carrying two C282Y alleles. In women, regular menstrual blood loss can delay iron accumulation, making excess iron more likely to become apparent after menopause.

The rs855791 A allele (T on the negative strand) alters TMPRSS6 function and is associated with reduced iron absorption, lower circulating iron and slightly lower hemoglobin levels. Its effect can become more important in women with substantial menstrual blood loss, increasing susceptibility to low iron status and iron-deficiency anemia.

The rs1799941 A allele (T on the negative strand) is associated with higher circulating SHBG levels. Higher SHBG increases testosterone binding in the circulation and can reduce the proportion of testosterone that is freely available to tissues, influencing overall androgen availability.

The rs6258 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the Pro185Leu substitution in SHBG and is associated with lower circulating SHBG levels and altered testosterone binding. This can affect the proportion of free testosterone and may also influence the accuracy of calculated free testosterone estimates based on standard SHBG measurements.

The rs523349 G allele is associated with altered activity of 5α-reductase type 2, the enzyme that converts testosterone into the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT). This can affect how efficiently testosterone is converted to DHT and therefore influence DHT-dependent androgen activity, although the effect of this common variant is relatively small.

The rs1799983 T allele (A on the negative strand) alters endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and has been associated with reduced nitric oxide availability. Nitric oxide is essential for relaxation and dilation of penile blood vessels, and reduced nitric oxide signalling may increase susceptibility to erectile dysfunction.

The rs10835638 T allele (A on the negative strand) reduces FSHB gene expression and is associated with lower circulating follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels. Lower FSH signalling can reduce stimulation of Sertoli cells, influencing testicular function, inhibin B production and sperm production, with the strongest effects seen in men carrying two T alleles.

The rs6166 C allele (G on the negative strand) causes the Asn680Ser substitution in the FSH receptor, which mediates the effects of FSH on Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis. This variant may influence individual sensitivity to FSH and male reproductive function, although its effects are small and not consistently observed across studies.

The rs6025 T allele (A on the negative strand), known as Factor V Leiden, makes factor V resistant to normal breakdown by activated protein C. Factor V therefore remains procoagulant for longer, increasing thrombin generation and the risk of venous thrombosis. This inherited thrombophilia is clinically important when considering testosterone replacement therapy, which requires additional caution in men with an increased thrombotic risk.

The rs1799963 A allele (T on the negative strand), known as the prothrombin G20210A variant, increases prothrombin production and circulating prothrombin levels. This promotes greater thrombin generation and increases susceptibility to venous thrombosis. The presence of an inherited thrombophilia is clinically important when considering testosterone replacement therapy and assessing overall thrombotic risk.

The rs1800562 A allele (T on the negative strand), known as HFE C282Y, can increase intestinal iron absorption and, particularly when present in two copies, lead to progressive iron accumulation. Significant iron overload can impair pituitary and testicular function, contributing to reduced testosterone production and hypogonadism in affected men.

The rs7903146 T allele (A on the negative strand) is associated with reduced insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells and a higher susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. Its effect appears to involve altered regulation of TCF7L2, a transcription factor involved in glucose metabolism and normal beta-cell function.

The rs10830963 G allele is associated with stronger or prolonged melatonin signalling in pancreatic beta cells, which can suppress insulin release and contribute to higher fasting glucose levels. Carriers have a modestly increased susceptibility to impaired glucose regulation and type 2 diabetes, particularly when food intake overlaps with periods of elevated melatonin.

The rs5219 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the E23K substitution in the Kir6.2 subunit of the pancreatic beta-cell potassium channel. The variant can alter the cell’s response to glucose and reduce glucose-stimulated insulin release, contributing to a modest increase in susceptibility to type 2 diabetes.

The rs13266634 C allele (G on the negative strand) encodes the R325 form of ZnT8, a zinc transporter involved in insulin storage and secretion in pancreatic beta cells. This allele is consistently associated with a modestly increased susceptibility to type 2 diabetes, likely through differences in beta-cell zinc handling and insulin processing.

The rs1801282 G allele causes the Pro12Ala substitution in PPARG and is associated with improved insulin sensitivity and a modestly lower susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. PPARG is a key regulator of adipocyte function, lipid storage and glucose metabolism, and the Ala12 variant appears to modestly improve metabolic regulation.

The rs2642438 A allele (T on the negative strand) causes the A165T substitution in MTARC1 and is associated with lower liver fat and reduced susceptibility to chronic liver disease and fibrosis. The precise molecular mechanism is not fully established, but the variant appears to influence hepatic lipid metabolism and provides a modest protective effect against fatty liver disease progression.

The rs2943641 C allele (G on the negative strand) is associated with reduced IRS1-related insulin signalling in skeletal muscle, contributing to lower insulin sensitivity and compensatory higher insulin levels. This increases susceptibility to insulin resistance and modestly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes.

The rs1260326 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the P446L substitution in GCKR and alters the regulation of glucokinase in the liver. It is associated with lower fasting glucose, improved insulin sensitivity and a modestly lower risk of type 2 diabetes, but also with higher triglyceride levels, reflecting a metabolic trade-off between glucose and lipid metabolism.

The rs560887 C allele (G on the negative strand) is associated with higher fasting glucose by influencing glucose regulation in pancreatic beta cells and the threshold for insulin secretion. It primarily affects the normal set point of fasting glucose rather than substantially increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

The rs3135506 C allele causes the Ser19Trp substitution in APOA5, a protein that plays an important role in triglyceride metabolism. The Trp19 variant can reduce the efficient secretion of APOA5 into the bloodstream, contributing to higher circulating triglyceride levels and increased susceptibility to hypertriglyceridemia.

The rs738409 G allele causes the I148M substitution in PNPLA3, impairing normal triglyceride breakdown in liver cells and promoting fat accumulation in the liver. It is one of the strongest common genetic risk variants for fatty liver disease and is associated not only with greater liver fat but also with increased susceptibility to steatohepatitis, fibrosis and progression to more advanced liver disease.

The rs58542926 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the E167K substitution in TM6SF2, reducing the liver’s ability to export triglycerides in lipoprotein particles and promoting fat accumulation within the liver. It increases susceptibility to fatty liver disease and liver damage, while paradoxically being associated with lower circulating triglyceride and LDL cholesterol levels.

The rs641738 T allele (A on the negative strand), located near MBOAT7, is associated with reduced hepatic MBOAT7 expression and altered phospholipid metabolism in the liver. It is associated with a modest increase in liver fat and susceptibility to fatty liver disease and fibrosis, with the most consistent evidence reported in populations of European ancestry.

The rs9939609 A allele is one of the best-established common genetic variants associated with higher body weight and obesity susceptibility. It marks a regulatory region within the FTO locus that influences pathways controlling energy balance and fat-cell biology, contributing to a modest tendency toward greater fat accumulation.

The rs17782313 C allele (G on the negative strand), located near MC4R, is associated with higher BMI and a modestly increased susceptibility to obesity. The MC4R pathway plays a central role in brain regulation of appetite, satiety and energy balance, although the direct functional effect of this particular variant has not been fully established.

The rs6548238 C allele (G on the negative strand), located near TMEM18, is associated with higher BMI and a modestly increased susceptibility to obesity. The TMEM18 locus is involved in pathways regulating body weight and energy balance, although the direct functional effect of this particular variant has not been fully established.

The rs174547 C allele (G on the negative strand) is associated with lower fatty acid desaturase activity and less efficient conversion of dietary precursor fatty acids into long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids. This can contribute to lower endogenous production of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids such as EPA, making circulating levels more dependent on direct dietary intake.

The rs1535 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with less efficient conversion of the plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid ALA into longer-chain omega-3 fatty acids such as EPA. This may increase reliance on direct dietary sources of EPA and other long-chain omega-3 fatty acids.

The rs10741657 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main marker of vitamin D status. CYP2R1 plays an important role in converting vitamin D into 25-hydroxyvitamin D in the liver, and carriers of the G allele have a modestly increased susceptibility to low vitamin D levels.

The rs2282679 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. The GC gene encodes vitamin D-binding protein, which transports vitamin D metabolites in the bloodstream, and genetic variation at this locus can influence measured vitamin D status.

The rs4680 A allele (T on the negative strand) causes the Val158Met substitution in COMT and reduces the activity of the enzyme that helps break down dopamine and other catecholamines. This can alter catecholamine signalling in brain regions involved in stress, emotion and cognitive control, although its effects on psychological traits are generally small and influenced by environmental factors.

The rs1360780 T allele (A on the negative strand) is associated with altered regulation of FKBP5, a protein involved in controlling the cellular response to the stress hormone cortisol. The variant can affect glucocorticoid-receptor feedback and has been linked to greater vulnerability to stress-related psychiatric outcomes, particularly in individuals exposed to significant early-life stress or trauma.

The rs6265 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the Val66Met substitution in BDNF and reduces activity-dependent release of BDNF in the brain. This can influence neuroplasticity, learning and memory, although its effects on mood and depression risk are small and strongly influenced by other genetic and environmental factors.

The rs1006737 A allele (T on the negative strand) can alter CACNA1C expression and the flow of calcium signals that regulate communication between brain cells. These changes may subtly influence neural circuits involved in mood regulation, stress response and cognitive processing.

The rs6295 C allele alters regulation of HTR1A, which encodes the serotonin 1A receptor involved in controlling serotonergic signalling in the brain. The variant can influence serotonin-system regulation and has been associated with susceptibility to depression and other mood disorders, although the effect is small and varies between populations.

The rs429358 C allele (G on the negative strand), when present together with rs7412-C, defines the APOE ε4 isoform. APOE ε4 influences lipid transport and amyloid-related processes in the brain and is associated with an increased susceptibility to cognitive decline and late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. However, carrying APOE ε4 does not mean that a person will develop Alzheimer’s disease, as cognitive ageing is influenced by many genetic, lifestyle and environmental factors.

The rs7412 C allele (G on the negative strand) should be interpreted together with rs429358 because these two variants define the major APOE isoforms. At rs7412, the alternative T allele contributes to the APOE ε2 isoform, which is generally associated with lower susceptibility to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, whereas the C allele can occur in either ε3 or ε4 and should not be interpreted as an independent cognitive risk allele.

The rs1800497 A allele (T on the negative strand) is associated with fewer available dopamine D2 receptors in brain regions involved in reward and motivation. With fewer D2 receptors available to respond to dopamine, reward signalling may be altered, potentially influencing how strongly a person responds to rewarding or reinforcing experiences, although the effect of this variant is small.

The rs16969968 A allele (T on the negative strand) causes the Asp398Asn substitution in the α5 subunit of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and alters normal receptor signalling. The variant is strongly associated with greater nicotine consumption and increased susceptibility to nicotine dependence.

The rs324420 A allele (T on the negative strand) reduces the activity of FAAH, an enzyme responsible for breaking down anandamide, one of the body’s natural endocannabinoids. As a result, anandamide can remain active for longer, strengthening endocannabinoid signalling involved in stress responses, emotional regulation and reward processing. The effect on addictive behaviours is small and varies between individuals and studies.

The rs1229984 T allele (A on the negative strand) produces a more active form of the ADH1B enzyme, causing alcohol to be converted into acetaldehyde more rapidly. Faster acetaldehyde production can increase unpleasant responses to alcohol, such as flushing, headache or stronger hangovers, and is generally associated with lower alcohol consumption and reduced susceptibility to alcohol dependence.

The rs671 A allele (T on the negative strand) markedly reduces the activity of the ALDH2 enzyme, which normally removes acetaldehyde produced during alcohol metabolism. As a result, acetaldehyde can accumulate after drinking, causing facial flushing, increased heart rate, nausea and other symptoms of alcohol intolerance, which often leads to lower alcohol consumption.

The rs1801198 G allele is associated with lower levels of holotranscobalamin, the biologically active form of vitamin B12 that delivers the vitamin to cells. This may reduce cellular vitamin B12 availability and influence homocysteine metabolism, particularly when vitamin B12 status is already low. Adequate vitamin B12 availability is important for normal nervous-system function, including processes supporting cognition, mood and neurological health.

The rs1801133 A allele (T on the negative strand) reduces MTHFR enzyme activity, making the conversion of folate into its active methylation-related form less efficient. This can contribute to lower folate availability and higher homocysteine levels, particularly when folate status is low, potentially affecting methylation and neurotransmitter-related processes important for normal mood and cognitive function.

The rs1801131 G allele (C on the negative strand) moderately reduces MTHFR enzyme activity and can make folate-dependent methylation less efficient. Its effect is smaller than that of rs1801133, but it may become more relevant when combined with other MTHFR variants or low folate status, potentially influencing methylation processes important for normal brain and neurotransmitter function.

The rs10741657 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with less efficient vitamin D metabolism and lower circulating levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D. This can increase susceptibility to low vitamin D status, which may be relevant to normal brain function, mood and cognition, particularly when vitamin D levels are already insufficient.

The rs2282679 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D by influencing vitamin D-binding protein and the transport of vitamin D metabolites in the bloodstream. This can increase susceptibility to low vitamin D status, which may be relevant to normal brain function, mood and cognition, particularly when vitamin D levels are insufficient.

The rs174547 C allele (G on the negative strand) is associated with lower FADS1 desaturase activity, reducing the efficiency with which dietary fatty-acid precursors are converted into long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids. These fatty acids are important components of brain-cell membranes and support normal neuronal signalling, so less efficient production may increase reliance on direct dietary sources of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids such as EPA and DHA.

The rs1535 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower FADS2-related desaturase activity, making the conversion of dietary omega-3 and omega-6 precursors into longer-chain fatty acids less efficient. Because long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids contribute to brain-cell membranes and neuronal signalling, carriers may rely more strongly on direct dietary sources of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids such as EPA and DHA.

The rs2476601 A allele (T on the negative strand) causes the R620W substitution in PTPN22 and alters the regulation of immune-cell signalling. This can weaken normal control of self-reactive immune cells, increasing susceptibility to several autoimmune diseases.

The rs7574865 T allele (A on the negative strand) is associated with increased STAT4 activity and stronger signalling through immune pathways that promote inflammatory immune responses. This can make immune activation more persistent and increase susceptibility to systemic autoimmune diseases, particularly rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

The rs2230926 G allele (C on the negative strand) causes the F127C substitution in the A20 protein and can reduce its ability to switch off NF-κB inflammatory signalling. This can allow immune activation and inflammation to persist for longer, increasing susceptibility to autoimmune disease.

The rs1990760 T allele (A on the negative strand) produces the Thr946 form of the MDA5 immune sensor and can increase interferon signalling in response to RNA. This may strengthen antiviral immune responses but can also make immune activation more persistent, contributing to increased susceptibility to autoimmune disease.

The rs3184504 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the R262W substitution in SH2B3 and reduces its ability to limit immune-cell signalling. This can allow stronger cytokine signalling and greater activation of immune cells, increasing susceptibility to autoimmune and inflammatory conditions.

The rs34536443 C allele causes the P1104A substitution in TYK2 and markedly reduces its kinase activity. This weakens inflammatory cytokine signalling and provides substantial protection against several autoimmune diseases. However, individuals carrying two copies of the C allele may have increased susceptibility to tuberculosis because some TYK2-dependent antimicrobial immune responses are impaired.

The rs2187668 T allele (A on the negative strand) is a genetic marker for the HLA-DQ2.5 haplotype, which increases susceptibility to celiac disease. HLA-DQ2.5 can efficiently present gluten-derived peptides to immune cells, allowing an abnormal immune response to gluten to develop in genetically susceptible individuals. Carrying this allele indicates genetic predisposition but does not mean that celiac disease will develop.

The rs7454108 C allele is a genetic marker for the HLA-DQ8 haplotype, which increases susceptibility to celiac disease. HLA-DQ8 can present gluten-derived peptides to immune cells, allowing an abnormal immune response to gluten to develop in genetically susceptible individuals. Carrying this allele indicates genetic predisposition but does not mean that celiac disease will develop.

The rs2066844 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the R702W substitution in NOD2 and reduces its ability to respond normally to components of intestinal bacteria. This can impair bacterial sensing and regulation of immune responses in the gut, increasing susceptibility to Crohn’s disease.

The rs2066845 C allele causes the G908R substitution in NOD2 and reduces normal recognition and handling of bacterial signals in the intestine. This can disrupt regulation of the gut immune response and increase susceptibility to Crohn’s disease.

The rs2241880 G allele (C on the negative strand) causes the T300A substitution in ATG16L1 and makes the cellular removal of intestinal bacteria through autophagy less efficient. This can impair bacterial clearance and disturb immune balance in the intestinal lining, contributing to increased susceptibility to Crohn’s disease.

The rs1061170 C allele (G on the negative strand) causes the Y402H substitution in complement factor H and alters its ability to regulate complement activation on retinal tissues. This can promote persistent complement-mediated inflammation and tissue damage in the retina, substantially increasing susceptibility to age-related macular degeneration.

The rs10741657 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with less efficient vitamin D metabolism and lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. This can increase susceptibility to low vitamin D status, potentially reducing vitamin D-dependent regulation of immune-cell activity and inflammatory responses when vitamin D levels are insufficient.

The rs2282679 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels by influencing vitamin D-binding protein and the transport of vitamin D metabolites in the bloodstream. This can increase susceptibility to low vitamin D status, potentially affecting vitamin D-dependent regulation of immune and inflammatory responses.

The rs1815739 T allele (A on the negative strand) introduces a premature stop signal in ACTN3, reducing production of α-actinin-3, a protein normally found in fast-twitch muscle fibres. Individuals with two T alleles lack α-actinin-3 completely, which can modestly reduce the muscle characteristics that favour rapid, powerful contractions and sprint/power performance.

The rs17602729 A allele (T on the negative strand) introduces a premature stop signal in AMPD1 and reduces the activity of AMP deaminase in skeletal muscle. Reduced enzyme activity can make rapid energy recycling during intense exercise less efficient, increasing susceptibility to early muscle fatigue, cramps or exercise-related muscle discomfort, particularly in individuals carrying two copies of the allele.

The rs1805086 C allele (G on the negative strand) causes the K153R substitution in myostatin, a protein that normally limits skeletal muscle growth. The variant has been associated with greater muscle mass or strength-related traits in some studies, but its functional effect is small and findings are not sufficiently consistent to consider it a strong muscle-growth variant.

The rs3736228 T allele (A on the negative strand) causes the A1330V substitution in LRP5 and reduces Wnt signalling involved in stimulating bone formation. This can contribute to lower bone mineral density and modestly increase susceptibility to osteoporosis and fractures, particularly when other bone-health risk factors are present.

The rs12722 T allele (A on the negative strand) may alter regulation of COL5A1, which contributes to the structure and mechanical properties of tendons and ligaments. This allele has been associated with differences in connective-tissue flexibility and a modestly increased susceptibility to tendon injury, although the effect is small and varies between studies.

The rs143383 A allele (T on the negative strand) reduces GDF5 expression, resulting in less production of a growth factor important for maintaining cartilage and joint tissues. Lower GDF5 activity can modestly reduce the capacity of joint tissues to maintain and repair cartilage, contributing to increased susceptibility to osteoarthritis over time.

The rs4680 A allele (T on the negative strand) produces the Met158 form of COMT, which has lower enzyme activity and breaks down dopamine and other catecholamines more slowly. This can alter the neural pathways that regulate pain and is associated with a modest tendency toward greater pain sensitivity in some situations, although the effect varies considerably between individuals.

The rs10741657 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with less efficient vitamin D metabolism and lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. This can increase susceptibility to low vitamin D status, which may become relevant to bone strength and normal muscle function when vitamin D levels are insufficient.

The rs2282679 G allele (C on the negative strand) is associated with lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels through variation in the vitamin D-binding protein pathway. This can increase susceptibility to low vitamin D status, which may become relevant to maintaining normal bone strength and muscle function when vitamin D levels are insufficient.

The rs855791 A allele (T on the negative strand) produces the Val736 form of TMPRSS6, which is less effective at suppressing the iron-regulating hormone hepcidin. This can reduce iron absorption and availability for red blood cell production, contributing to slightly lower iron stores and hemoglobin levels and potentially affecting oxygen transport and physical endurance when iron status is already low.

The rs12248560 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP2C19*17, increases production of the CYP2C19 enzyme. This can make some medicines leave the body faster. For example, citalopram and escitalopram levels may be lower, which can reduce their antidepressant effect; omeprazole or lansoprazole may suppress stomach acid less; and voriconazole levels may be too low for reliable treatment. Clopidogrel is different: CYP2C19 activates it, so greater activity can form more active drug. This SNP alone does not establish a person's overall CYP2C19 activity; both gene copies and other variants matter.

The rs12769205 G allele (C on the opposite strand), part of CYP2C19*35, interferes with normal RNA splicing and is classified as a no-function change. If this allele is present, that gene copy makes little or no working enzyme. This may reduce activation of clopidogrel and slow the breakdown of other CYP2C19 medicines. The variant is especially relevant in people with African ancestry. Its effect must be combined with the other CYP2C19 variants to determine the person's predicted metabolizer type.

The rs28399504 G allele (C on the opposite strand), called CYP2C19*4, disrupts the gene's start signal, so the affected copy is not expected to make a working enzyme. This can reduce clopidogrel activation and slow the breakdown of medicines normally cleared by CYP2C19. The variant is rare, and one result alone cannot determine a person's overall metabolizer type; the other CYP2C19 copy and relevant variants must also be assessed.

The rs41291556 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called CYP2C19*8, changes the enzyme's amino-acid sequence. Laboratory studies suggest that it can substantially reduce enzyme activity, but clinical evidence for this rare allele is limited. If the change reduces activity, clopidogrel activation may be lower and some other CYP2C19 medicines may be cleared more slowly. The result should be interpreted with the complete CYP2C19 genotype, not as a stand-alone prediction.

The rs4244285 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called CYP2C19*2, disrupts RNA splicing and usually leaves that gene copy with little or no working enzyme. With clopidogrel, less active medicine may be formed, weakening its effect on platelets. For medicines CYP2C19 normally breaks down, reduced activity can instead raise drug levels and side-effect risk. The clinical meaning depends on both CYP2C19 copies and the medicine being used.

The rs4986893 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called CYP2C19*3, creates an early stop in the enzyme's instructions, so that gene copy cannot make working CYP2C19. This can reduce clopidogrel activation and slow the breakdown of other CYP2C19 medicines. The variant is more frequent in East Asian populations than in European populations. Its effect is determined together with the other CYP2C19 copy and variants.

The rs72552267 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called CYP2C19*6, changes the enzyme in a way that has abolished its activity in laboratory testing. The affected gene copy is therefore treated as a no-function allele: it may reduce clopidogrel activation and slow the breakdown of other CYP2C19 medicines. Because this allele is very rare, its clinical meaning depends on confirming the result and interpreting the full CYP2C19 genotype.

The rs12777823 A allele lies between genes in the CYP2C region; it is not a CYP2C9 star-allele change. In people with African ancestry, it is associated with needing a lower warfarin dose, even after accounting for common CYP2C9 variants. The same relationship has not been established consistently in other ancestry groups. It is one input to a warfarin dose estimate and should be interpreted with ancestry, other genes, clinical factors, and INR monitoring.

The rs1057910 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called CYP2C9*3, markedly reduces CYP2C9 activity. The body can therefore clear warfarin's more active S-form, acenocoumarol, phenytoin, and some other medicines more slowly. Their levels or effects may rise, increasing bleeding with coumarins or toxicity with phenytoin; lower starting doses may be needed. The size of the change depends on both CYP2C9 copies and the specific medicine, and warfarin dosing is guided by INR.

The rs1799853 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP2C9*2, reduces but does not usually abolish enzyme activity. Some medicines, including warfarin, acenocoumarol, phenytoin, and several anti-inflammatory drugs, may be cleared more slowly and remain in the body longer. This can increase their effect or side-effect risk, so the impact depends on the medicine and the other CYP2C9 copy. Coumarin dosing also uses clinical monitoring such as INR.

The rs28371685 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP2C9*11, reduces the enzyme's ability to clear some medicines. For drugs such as warfarin and phenytoin, this may increase exposure and alter the dose needed. The allele is more relevant in people with African ancestry, and evidence is more limited than for the common *2 and *3 alleles. It should be interpreted with the full CYP2C9 genotype and the medicine-specific clinical context.

The rs28371686 G allele (C on the opposite strand), called CYP2C9*5, reduces CYP2C9 activity. Medicines cleared by this enzyme, including warfarin and phenytoin, may therefore remain in the body longer, potentially increasing their effects or adverse effects. This allele is more frequent in people with African ancestry than in many European groups. Its contribution is combined with other CYP2C9 alleles when predicting drug handling.

The rs7900194 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called CYP2C9*8, reduces CYP2C9 activity. This can slow the clearance of medicines such as warfarin and may lower the dose needed to achieve the intended effect. The allele is particularly relevant in people with African ancestry. It should be interpreted alongside the other CYP2C9 alleles and, for warfarin, the patient's INR and clinical circumstances.

The rs9332131 deletion, called CYP2C9*6, shifts the gene's reading frame and is expected to leave that copy without working enzyme. Medicines cleared by CYP2C9, including warfarin and phenytoin, may then be cleared more slowly, increasing their effect or toxicity risk. The deletion occurs mainly in people with African ancestry. Because this site has nearby insertion/deletion variation, the laboratory must identify the exact allele; the result is interpreted with the other CYP2C9 copy.

The rs2108622 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP4F2*3, reduces the enzyme's breakdown of vitamin K. With more vitamin K available to support clotting-factor production, some people need a somewhat higher warfarin dose to reach the same anticoagulation effect. This is usually a modest contribution and is considered together with VKORC1, CYP2C9, and clinical INR measurements.

The rs9923231 T allele corresponds to VKORC1 -1639A on the opposite strand and lowers production of VKORC1, the protein that recycles vitamin K and is inhibited by warfarin and related medicines. With less VKORC1 available, a lower coumarin dose may produce the same anticoagulant effect. The result contributes to dose prediction for warfarin and other coumarins, together with CYP2C9, other factors, and INR monitoring; it is not a measure of how quickly the drug is metabolized.

The rs2231142 T allele (A on the opposite strand) changes the ABCG2/BCRP transporter and reduces its ability to move substances out of cells. Rosuvastatin may consequently reach higher blood levels, which can increase the chance of muscle side effects. The same transporter also handles urate and allopurinol-related compounds, and this variant has been linked to differences in urate levels and allopurinol response. The result is one factor in medicine-specific assessment, not a stand-alone dose instruction.

The rs2306283 G allele (C on the opposite strand) changes the SLCO1B1/OATP1B1 transporter, but it does not by itself establish reduced transporter function or statin-related muscle risk. Its main value here is to help identify the SLCO1B1 haplotype when read with rs4149056. Those variants together distinguish common transporter forms, including forms that transport statins less efficiently. This row should therefore be interpreted as part of a haplotype, not as an independent risk result.

The rs4149056 C allele (G on the opposite strand), part of SLCO1B1*5, reduces the OATP1B1 transporter's movement of statins from blood into the liver, where they are taken up and processed. More statin can remain in the blood and reach muscle, increasing the chance of muscle pain or injury. The effect is strongest for simvastatin and differs among statins. The complete SLCO1B1 genotype and the particular statin determine the interpretation.

The rs112766203 A allele has shown a possible effect on DPYD enzyme activity in laboratory work, but the link to fluorouracil or capecitabine toxicity in patients is not established well enough to predict a dose change. It should not be treated on its own as a proven reduced-function allele. Clinical interpretation requires a validated DPYD variant and the combined activity score from both gene copies.

The rs115232898 C allele (G on the opposite strand), part of DPYD*6, reduces the activity of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD), the main enzyme that breaks down fluorouracil and capecitabine. Slower breakdown can expose the body to more medicine and raise the risk of severe toxicity, including low blood counts, diarrhoea, and mouth sores. This allele is most relevant in people with African ancestry. Dose decisions use the combined DPYD activity score, not this variant alone.

The rs146356975 C allele (G on the opposite strand) is associated with reduced DPYD activity. Because DPD helps clear fluorouracil and capecitabine, reduced activity can allow these medicines to build up and increase the risk of serious side effects. The variant is uncommon, so the result should be interpreted using current DPYD guidance and combined with the other DPYD copy to estimate overall enzyme function.

The rs3918290 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called DPYD*2A, disrupts RNA splicing and prevents that gene copy from making working DPD enzyme. DPD normally clears most fluorouracil and capecitabine; reduced function can therefore cause severe or even life-threatening toxicity at usual doses. The safe starting approach depends on the activity score from both DPYD copies, and some predicted poor metabolizers should avoid these medicines.

The rs55886062 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called DPYD*13, is a no-function allele: the altered enzyme cannot adequately break down fluorouracil or capecitabine. One affected copy can substantially increase toxicity risk and usually leads clinicians to start with a reduced dose; two no-function copies may make an alternative treatment necessary. The decision is based on the combined DPYD activity score. A negative result at this site does not rule out other causes of reduced DPD activity.

The rs56038477 T allele is a synonymous change, so it does not alter the DPD protein by itself. It can mark the DPYD HapB3 chromosome, which contains a separate splice-altering variant that reduces enzyme activity. The result is therefore useful as a haplotype marker, not as an independent toxicity allele. If both markers for the same HapB3 chromosome are tested, they must not be counted as two separate reduced-function alleles.

The rs67376798 A allele changes the DPD protein and reduces its ability to break down fluorouracil and capecitabine. These medicines may then remain in the body longer, increasing the risk of severe toxicity. A reduced starting dose may be appropriate, but the amount depends on the combined DPYD activity score from both gene copies and is adjusted with clinical monitoring.

The rs75017182 C allele (G on the opposite strand) is the functional splice-altering change associated with DPYD HapB3. It causes some DPYD RNA to be processed incorrectly, reducing the amount of working DPD enzyme. Fluorouracil and capecitabine may then be cleared more slowly, increasing toxicity risk. The variant contributes to the overall DPYD activity score; dose interpretation should use current clinical guidance because allele-score recommendations can be updated.

The rs116855232 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called NUDT15*3, reduces the enzyme's ability to detoxify thioguanine compounds formed from azathioprine, mercaptopurine, and thioguanine. More of these compounds can enter DNA in bone-marrow cells, causing severe drops in white blood cells and other blood-cell counts. The risk is greatest when both gene copies have no function. NUDT15 and TPMT results are interpreted together before thiopurine treatment.

The rs147390019 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called NUDT15*4, is assigned no function based on clinical evidence. Like other no-function NUDT15 alleles, it can leave more active thioguanine compounds available to damage bone-marrow cells during azathioprine, mercaptopurine, or thioguanine treatment. This can cause severe low blood counts. The effect depends on both NUDT15 copies and TPMT status; the individual SNP is not a dose by itself.

The rs1142345 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called TPMT*3C, destabilizes the TPMT enzyme and reduces its ability to divert thiopurine medicines into less active products. More active thioguanine compounds can then accumulate in bone marrow, increasing the risk of dangerously low blood counts during azathioprine, mercaptopurine, or thioguanine treatment. Read it with rs1800460 to establish whether the changes are on one or both gene copies, and assess NUDT15 as well.

The rs1800460 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called TPMT*3B, reduces TPMT activity. In many people of European ancestry it is inherited on the same chromosome as rs1142345, forming TPMT*3A; together these changes can leave that gene copy with little or no activity. Reduced TPMT function allows active thiopurine compounds to build up in bone marrow and cause severe low blood counts. The two sites must be phased, and NUDT15 also contributes to risk.

The rs1800462 G allele (C on the opposite strand), called TPMT*2, makes the TPMT enzyme nonfunctional. TPMT normally diverts azathioprine, mercaptopurine, and thioguanine away from active thioguanine compounds. When TPMT activity is low, those compounds can accumulate in bone marrow and cause severe, potentially life-threatening suppression of blood-cell production. Risk and dosing depend on whether one or both copies are affected and on NUDT15 status.

The rs1800584 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called TPMT*4, affects RNA splicing and is expected to reduce the amount of working TPMT enzyme. If activity is reduced, active thiopurine compounds may accumulate in bone marrow and increase the risk of low blood counts during azathioprine, mercaptopurine, or thioguanine treatment. The clinical prediction depends on the complete TPMT genotype and NUDT15 status; this rare variant is not interpreted alone.

The rs4148323 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called UGT1A1*6, reduces the enzyme's ability to attach glucuronic acid to bilirubin and SN-38, the active breakdown product of irinotecan. Less SN-38 is inactivated, so exposure can rise and severe neutropenia or diarrhoea becomes more likely during irinotecan treatment. The effect is especially relevant in East Asian populations. Risk is assessed from both UGT1A1 copies and the treatment context.

The rs887829 T allele (A on the opposite strand) is a marker for the UGT1A1*28 promoter-repeat allele in many people, rather than the repeat itself. When it tracks with *28, lower UGT1A1 production can slow the inactivation of bilirubin and irinotecan's active product, SN-38. This may increase jaundice with some medicines and severe neutropenia or diarrhoea with irinotecan. Linkage between the marker and *28 varies by ancestry, so the marker alone does not always establish the UGT1A1 haplotype.

The rs1058164 G allele (C on the opposite strand) is one component used to identify the reduced-function CYP2D6*29 haplotype. That haplotype can lower CYP2D6 activity, which may reduce activation of codeine and tramadol and alter the handling of other CYP2D6 medicines. This single site has no reliable stand-alone interpretation: it must be read with the other *29-defining variants, the rest of the CYP2D6 genotype, and gene copy number.

The rs1065852 A allele (T on the opposite strand) contributes to the reduced-function CYP2D6*10 allele. Lower CYP2D6 activity can reduce conversion of codeine and tramadol into their stronger pain-relieving forms, while also slowing clearance of some other medicines. The effect varies by drug and by the other CYP2D6 allele. A reliable prediction requires the full diplotype and copy-number assessment, especially because CYP2D6 can have deletions or extra copies.

The rs1135840 G allele (C on the opposite strand) usually has little effect on CYP2D6 activity by itself. It helps define the background of several CYP2D6 star alleles, including reduced-function forms such as *10 and *41. Its value is therefore in assigning the correct haplotype; it should not be reported as an independent drug-response risk allele. A complete interpretation also requires other CYP2D6 variants and gene copy number.

The rs16947 A allele (T on the opposite strand) has limited functional meaning on its own, but it is a key marker for identifying several CYP2D6 star alleles, including *2, *17, *29, and *41. Those haplotypes can have different levels of enzyme activity and therefore different effects on medicines such as codeine, tramadol, and many antidepressants. This SNP supports haplotype assignment rather than an independent risk prediction; copy-number and other CYP2D6 changes must also be assessed.

The rs28371706 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called CYP2D6*17, reduces CYP2D6 activity. The size of the effect differs among medicines, so it may change the activation of codeine or tramadol and the clearance of other CYP2D6 substrates by different amounts. This allele is most relevant in people with African ancestry. It must be combined with the other CYP2D6 allele and copy-number results before a metabolizer type can be assigned.

The rs28371725 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP2D6*41, disrupts RNA processing so that less working enzyme is produced. This contributes reduced CYP2D6 activity, which can alter the handling of medicines such as codeine, tramadol, antidepressants, and some antipsychotics. Its contribution to the predicted metabolizer type depends on the other allele and any CYP2D6 gene copies or hybrid genes; interpretation should use current activity-value tables.

The rs35742686 deletion, called CYP2D6*3, shifts the gene's reading frame and prevents that copy from making working enzyme. If both CYP2D6 copies have no function, codeine and tramadol may not be converted efficiently to their active pain-relieving forms; other CYP2D6 medicines may also be cleared more slowly. A single deletion does not determine the overall phenotype. Both gene copies and CYP2D6 copy number must be assessed.

The rs3892097 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP2D6*4, disrupts RNA splicing and produces no working enzyme from that copy. With no functional CYP2D6 copies, codeine and tramadol may provide little pain relief because their active forms are not made efficiently; other CYP2D6 medicines can also accumulate. The clinical prediction depends on both gene copies and copy number, and is specific to each medicine.

The rs5030655 deletion, called CYP2D6*6, shifts the gene's reading frame and is expected to eliminate enzyme activity from that copy. This can reduce activation of codeine and tramadol and slow clearance of other CYP2D6 medicines. Whether it changes a person's predicted response depends on the second gene copy and on CYP2D6 deletions, duplications, or hybrid genes.

The rs5030656 deletion, called CYP2D6*9, removes three DNA bases and shortens the enzyme by one amino acid. It reduces, but does not usually eliminate, CYP2D6 activity. This can partly reduce codeine or tramadol activation and alter the clearance of other CYP2D6 medicines. The result contributes to the activity score together with the other allele and any gene copies.

The rs59421388 T allele (A on the opposite strand) is one of the changes used to identify the reduced-function CYP2D6*29 haplotype. *29 can lower enzyme activity and alter the activation or clearance of CYP2D6 medicines, but this SNP alone does not establish that haplotype or predict a drug response. It must be interpreted with the other *29 components, the wider CYP2D6 background, and gene copy number.

The rs61736512 T allele (A on the opposite strand) contributes to the multi-base CYP2D6*29 change together with rs1058164; rs59421388 and the surrounding allele background are also needed for haplotype assignment. The resulting *29 allele has reduced activity, which may alter the activation of codeine or tramadol and the clearance of other CYP2D6 medicines. Neither this SNP nor rs1058164 should be interpreted as an independent result.

The rs2395029 G allele is a marker that is often inherited with HLA-B*57:01; it is not the HLA allele itself. HLA-B*57:01 can cause a serious hypersensitivity reaction to abacavir, so confirmed carriers should not receive that medicine. Because linkage between the marker and HLA-B*57:01 is not perfect in every population, a positive marker should be confirmed by direct HLA-B*57:01 testing before it is used for a prescribing decision.

The rs1061235 T allele is a nearby marker for HLA-A*31:01, an HLA type associated with severe skin and other hypersensitivity reactions to carbamazepine. The marker can identify many carriers but may also be positive when HLA-A*31:01 is absent. A positive result therefore needs confirmation by HLA-A typing before it is treated as the drug-risk allele; the association concerns carbamazepine exposure, not a general allergy tendency.

The rs9263726 A allele has been studied as a possible marker for HLA-B*58:01, the HLA type associated with severe allopurinol skin reactions. The link was described mainly in East Asian populations and is incomplete; the evidence reviewed for this panel did not establish which rs9263726 allele reliably marks HLA-B*58:01. This SNP must not be used by itself to decide whether allopurinol is safe. Direct HLA-B*58:01 testing is needed.

The rs35599367 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called CYP3A4*22, is associated with lower CYP3A4 production. Medicines cleared by CYP3A4 may therefore remain in the body longer. This can contribute to higher exposure to drugs such as tacrolimus or quetiapine, but the effect depends on the medicine and other genes, especially CYP3A5 for tacrolimus. The variant is one part of a clinical prediction, not a dose instruction by itself.

The rs10264272 T allele (A on the opposite strand), called CYP3A5*6, disrupts RNA splicing and prevents that copy from making functional CYP3A5 enzyme. A person who has no functional CYP3A5 copies generally clears tacrolimus more slowly than a CYP3A5 expresser. To know whether a functional copy is present, this variant must be considered with CYP3A5*3, *7, and the other gene copy. Tacrolimus blood-level monitoring remains essential.

The rs41303343 insertion, called CYP3A5*7, shifts the gene's reading frame and leaves that copy unable to make functional enzyme. If no functional CYP3A5 copy remains, tacrolimus is generally cleared more slowly than in expressers, affecting the starting dose needed to reach target blood levels. The insertion must be interpreted with *3, *6, and the other CYP3A5 copy; blood-level monitoring guides the final dose.

The rs776746 T allele (A on the opposite strand) is the functional CYP3A5*1 form. People with at least one functioning CYP3A5 copy can clear tacrolimus faster and may have lower blood levels on a usual weight-based starting dose, so a higher starting dose may be needed under transplant-team monitoring. The other CYP3A5 copy and no-function variants such as *3, *6, and *7 determine whether a functional copy is present.

The rs28399499 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called CYP2B6*18, is a no-function allele. Because CYP2B6 helps clear efavirenz, reduced activity can raise efavirenz levels and increase side effects such as dizziness, vivid dreams, or mood changes. The overall effect depends on both CYP2B6 copies and other factors that affect the drug; this allele should not be treated as a complete prediction on its own.

The rs34223104 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called CYP2B6*22, lies in a control region and may increase CYP2B6 production. If that leads to faster efavirenz clearance, blood levels could be lower and treatment response could be affected. The functional evidence for this allele is less certain than for established loss-of-function alleles, so one SNP alone should not be used to infer a definite metabolizer type or change treatment.

The rs3745274 T allele (A on the opposite strand) is part of the reduced-function CYP2B6*6 allele. Because CYP2B6 is a major route for clearing efavirenz, reduced activity can raise drug levels and make nervous-system side effects, such as dizziness or vivid dreams, more likely. The effect depends on the other CYP2B6 variants and the patient's treatment; the complete genotype and clinical response guide interpretation.

The rs1050828 T allele (A on the opposite strand) contributes to the G6PD A-minus form when it occurs with rs1050829 on the same chromosome. Reduced G6PD activity weakens red blood cells' protection from oxidative stress, so some medicines can trigger their breakdown (haemolysis). This matters for drugs such as rasburicase, primaquine, and dapsone. G6PD is on the X chromosome, and enzyme testing is needed to determine actual activity, especially in people with two X chromosomes.

The rs1050829 C allele (G on the opposite strand) is used with rs1050828 to identify the G6PD A-minus form. On its own, it does not establish clinically important G6PD deficiency. When the two changes are on the same chromosome, they can reduce the red cell enzyme's ability to protect against oxidative stress and raise the risk of haemolysis with certain medicines. Direct G6PD enzyme-activity testing is needed to assess the person's functional status.

The rs5030868 A allele (T on the opposite strand), associated with the G6PD Mediterranean form, can markedly reduce the enzyme activity that protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. During exposure to certain oxidising medicines, red cells may break down, causing acute haemolytic anaemia. The exact risk depends on the person's measured enzyme activity, dose, and exposure. Because G6PD is X-linked, genotype does not always predict enzyme activity in people with two X chromosomes; an activity test is important.

The rs267606617 G allele corresponds to the mitochondrial m.1555A>G variant in MT-RNR1. It changes the mitochondrial ribosome so that aminoglycoside antibiotics can bind more like they do to bacterial ribosomes. Exposure to gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin, or related drugs can then cause sudden, permanent hearing loss, even at usual drug levels. The variant is passed through the maternal line. Aminoglycosides are generally avoided when a safe, effective alternative is available.

The rs267606618 C allele corresponds to MT-RNR1 m.1095T>C. This mitochondrial ribosomal change is associated with increased susceptibility to permanent hearing loss from aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin and amikacin. The evidence is less extensive than for m.1555A>G, but current guidance treats a detected increased-risk variant seriously because the harm can be irreversible. The variant is maternally inherited and may be present in only some mitochondrial copies.

The rs267606619 T allele corresponds to MT-RNR1 m.1494C>T. It changes the mitochondrial ribosome in a way that can make aminoglycoside antibiotics more damaging to the inner ear, raising the risk of permanent hearing loss. Current guidance recommends avoiding these antibiotics in carriers when a suitable alternative exists, unless the infection makes treatment necessary. Mitochondrial variants are passed through the maternal line, and the proportion of affected mitochondrial copies can vary.

The rs1041983 T allele is a synonymous NAT2 change, meaning it does not alter the enzyme's amino-acid sequence. It helps distinguish NAT2 haplotypes, but does not by itself make someone a fast or slow acetylator. NAT2 acetylator status is determined from the combination of variants on both gene copies; this marker mainly improves the accuracy of naming those haplotypes.

The rs1208 A allele changes the NAT2 protein but is mainly useful for distinguishing haplotypes that otherwise look alike. It does not by itself establish faster or slower acetylation or predict a medicine response. The complete set of NAT2 variants on both gene copies determines acetylator status, which is clinically relevant for medicines such as hydralazine.

The rs1799929 T allele is a synonymous NAT2 change and has no established effect on enzyme activity by itself. It helps distinguish some NAT2 haplotypes, but cannot show whether a person is a slow, intermediate, or rapid acetylator alone. That status depends on the combination of functional variants inherited on both copies of NAT2.

The rs1799930 A allele, commonly associated with NAT2*6, reduces the enzyme's ability to acetylate hydralazine. People with reduced activity may clear hydralazine more slowly and have higher drug levels, which can increase both blood-pressure-lowering effects and adverse effects such as drug-induced lupus. This SNP contributes to the predicted acetylator type; the other NAT2 copy must also be assessed.

The rs1799931 A allele, commonly associated with NAT2*7, reduces NAT2 acetylation activity. For hydralazine, a slow-acetylator genotype can lead to higher drug levels and a greater chance of adverse effects, including a lupus-like reaction. The allele is more frequent in some East Asian populations. A person's predicted acetylator status is based on both NAT2 copies, not this variant alone.

The rs1801279 A allele, associated with NAT2*14, reduces NAT2 activity. This allele is more relevant in people with African ancestry. If both NAT2 copies confer slow acetylation, hydralazine can remain at higher levels, potentially increasing its blood-pressure effect and adverse effects such as drug-induced lupus. The full NAT2 diplotype is needed to predict acetylator status; this SNP alone is not a clinical result.

The rs1801280 C allele, associated with NAT2*5, reduces NAT2 activity and contributes to slow acetylation. For hydralazine, slower inactivation can increase drug exposure and the chance of adverse effects, including drug-induced lupus; CPIC recommendations are based on the combined NAT2 acetylator phenotype. NAT2 also processes other medicines, but hydralazine is the drug for which current CPIC guidance supports genotype-based prescribing.

The rs1799807 C allele (G on the opposite strand), called the atypical BCHE variant, reduces the enzyme's activity and its ability to act on succinylcholine. Because butyrylcholinesterase normally breaks down succinylcholine and mivacurium, these anaesthetic muscle relaxants may last longer in the body, prolonging paralysis and the need for breathing support. Risk is greatest when both gene copies are affected; the full BCHE genotype and enzyme activity help clarify the result.

The rs1803274 T allele, called BCHE*K, modestly reduces butyrylcholinesterase activity. BChE helps break down the muscle relaxants succinylcholine and mivacurium, so reduced activity can prolong paralysis and the need for breathing support after anaesthesia. This variant alone often has a small effect, but it can matter more with another damaging BCHE variant. Genotype does not replace clinical assessment or enzyme-activity testing.

The rs429358 C allele (G on the opposite strand) changes the ApoE protein. Together with rs7412-C, it defines the APOE ε4 form. People with two ε4 copies have a higher risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), including brain swelling or small areas of bleeding, when treated with anti-amyloid medicines such as lecanemab or donanemab. This SNP alone cannot determine ε4 status; both APOE sites must be read together.

The rs7412 C allele (G on the opposite strand) must be interpreted with rs429358 because the two sites together define the major APOE forms. At this position, T contributes to ε2, while C can be present in either ε3 or ε4. C therefore has no independent risk meaning, but it is part of the ε4 combination when rs429358 is also C. The two results together determine whether the higher ARIA risk associated especially with ε4/ε4 is relevant to anti-amyloid treatment.

The rs113994095 T allele (A on the opposite strand) causes the POLG p.Ala467Thr change, which can impair the enzyme that copies mitochondrial DNA. Two disease-causing POLG copies can cause a mitochondrial disorder; in that setting, valproate can trigger acute, potentially fatal liver failure and is contraindicated. Finding one copy alone does not diagnose POLG disease or automatically establish that valproate is contraindicated; symptoms, family history, and clinical genetic assessment matter.

The rs113994097 G allele (C on the opposite strand) causes POLG p.Trp748Ser, a disease-associated change in the enzyme that copies mitochondrial DNA. When a person has two disease-causing POLG copies, valproate can trigger acute, potentially fatal liver injury. This variant is distinct from p.Ala467Thr, although the two can occur together. One copy alone does not diagnose POLG-related disease or determine treatment; clinical assessment is required.

The rs671 A allele (T on the opposite strand), called ALDH2*2, greatly reduces the activity of the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, a substance formed when alcohol is broken down. Acetaldehyde can build up after drinking and cause facial flushing, headache, nausea, and a rapid heartbeat. The same enzyme helps activate nitroglycerin, so reduced activity may weaken its effect for angina. The size of these effects depends on the full ALDH2 genotype and clinical context.

The rs75527207 A allele (T on the opposite strand) causes the CFTR G551D change. The CFTR channel reaches the cell surface but does not open normally, reducing salt and water movement across the cell membrane. Ivacaftor can help this channel open, so the variant can indicate potential benefit from a CFTR modulator rather than increased drug toxicity. Treatment eligibility requires a confirmed cystic-fibrosis diagnosis and clinical-grade testing of the relevant CFTR variants.
